title: Odysseus' praise of feast and song
greek: τοῦτό τί μοι κάλλιστον ἐνὶ φρεσὶν εἴδεται εἶναι (touto ti moi kalliston eni phresin eidetai einai)
short: Odysseus opens his tale by praising the feast with a singer as the finest thing in life, a compliment to his Phaeacian hosts and their bard Demodocus.
body: Before he reveals his name, Odysseus answers Alcinous with a small hymn to the banquet: a whole people in festive joy (euphrosunē), guests seated in order, tables full, wine drawn from the mixing-bowl, and a singer (aoidos) whose voice is 'like unto the gods in voice'. Gregory Nagy reads telos ('fulfilment', Murray's 'fulfillment of delight') and kharis ('gratification') here as the vocabulary of a festival, in which song is the crowning event. The speech also sets up what follows: Books 9 to 12, the 'Apologoi', are Odysseus' own performance at such a feast, and at 11.368 Alcinous will praise him for telling his story 'as doth a minstrel'. Not every ancient reader approved. Plato's Socrates cites these lines about tables 'laden with bread and meat' as an example of poetry that does not teach self-control (Republic 3.390a-b).

anchor: I am Odysseus, son of Laertes
title: Odysseus names himself: wiles and kleos
greek: εἴμ᾽ Ὀδυσεὺς Λαερτιάδης, ὃς πᾶσι δόλοισιν / ἀνθρώποισι μέλω, καί μευ κλέος οὐρανὸν ἵκει (eim' Odyseus Laertiadēs, hos pasi doloisin anthrōpoisi melō, kai meu kleos ouranon hikei)
short: The long-delayed self-revelation: Odysseus is famous for his tricks (doloi), and his kleos, the fame carried by song, 'reaches heaven'.
body: Since landing on Scheria in Book 6 Odysseus has kept his name hidden; Alcinous asked for it at 8.550. The answer comes with a proud boast. The Greek says literally 'I am a concern (melō) to all men for my wiles', and Nagy points out that pasi ('all') can go both with 'wiles' and with 'men', and that melō is related to words for song (melos) and care. Kleos is the fame that poetry preserves, the reward of the Iliadic hero; Odysseus has just heard Demodocus sing his part in the Trojan Horse (8.499-520). The self-introduction frames the whole narrative of Books 9-12, in which naming becomes a matter of life and death: he will hide his name from the Cyclops as 'Noman' (9.366) and then ruinously reveal it (9.502-505).

title: Ithaca: 'clear-seen', lying 'toward the gloom'
greek: Ἰθάκην εὐδείελον ... πρὸς ζόφον (Ithakēn eudeielon ... pros zophon)
short: Odysseus' description of his island, with Mount Neriton and its neighbours, is the starting point of a long debate over which modern island Homer's Ithaca is.
body: Eudeielos probably means 'clear to see', 'conspicuous' (some take it as 'sunny' or 'lying to the west'); it is a standing epithet of islands. Odysseus lists Neriton, 'covered with waving forests' (einosiphyllon), and the nearby islands Dulichium, Same and Zacynthus, and then says that Ithaca lies 'low' (chthamalē) and 'furthest out to sea toward the gloom' (pros zophon), that is, toward the west, while the others lie toward the dawn. The modern island of Ithaki is neither low nor the westernmost of the group, so the passage has been argued over since antiquity. Merry and Riddell treat it in a separate appendix on Ithaca. In modern times W. Dörpfeld argued that Homer's Ithaca was Leukas, and R. Bittlestone, J. Diggle and J. Underhill (Odysseus Unbound, 2005) proposed the Paliki peninsula of Cephalonia; most scholars keep the traditional identification and allow for poetic geography. Note the emotional climax: 'no other thing can I see sweeter than one's own land' (9.27-28).

title: Nostos: the 'woeful homecoming' and the Apologoi
greek: νόστον ἐμὸν πολυκηδέ᾽ (noston emon polykēde')
short: With these words Odysseus begins the 'Apologoi', his first-person account of his wanderings that fills Books 9 to 12.
body: Nostos, 'return home', is the theme of the whole Odyssey and of a lost epic tradition of 'Returns' (Nostoi) of the Greek heroes from Troy; the poem's first lines call the day of return to Ithaca the thing Odysseus' companions lost (1.5-9). Here the adjective polykēdēs, 'full of cares', colours the whole tale before it starts. The ancient name for Books 9-12 was the Apologoi ('tales told to Alcinous'). The choice to let the hero narrate the fantastic adventures himself has been much discussed: everything we hear about Cyclopes, witches and monsters is told by a man famous for lies, at a feast, to an audience whose gifts he needs. Nagy argues that the episodes are organised around the link between nóos (mind, awareness) and nostos: whoever loses his mind, like the Lotus-eaters' victims, loses his return.

title: The Cicones and Ismarus
greek: Κικόνεσσι ... Ἰσμάρῳ (Kikonessi ... Ismarōi)
short: A Thracian people, Trojan allies in the Iliad; the first adventure is an ordinary piratical raid that turns into a defeat because the men will not leave.
body: The Cicones lived on the Thracian coast of the northern Aegean; the Iliad lists them among Troy's allies (Il. 2.846). Ismarus was their town, near later Maroneia. The episode belongs to the real world of the Aegean, unlike the wonders that follow after Cape Malea. It also sets the pattern for the books ahead: Odysseus gives a sensible order to leave, his men 'in their great folly' (the Greek calls them nēpioi, 'fools, childish') stay to drink and feast on the beach, and they pay for it, losing six men from each ship. The comparison of the counter-attacking Cicones to leaves and flowers in spring (9.51) echoes an Iliadic simile for armies (Il. 2.468). The raid also provides the wonderful wine of Maro (9.196-211) that will defeat the Cyclops.

title: The fair division of spoils
greek: ὡς μή τίς μοι ἀτεμβόμενος κίοι ἴσης (hōs mē tis moi atembomenos kioi isēs)
short: Odysseus shares the booty so that no man goes 'cheated of his equal share', a leader's duty that recurs at the end of the book.
body: In Homeric warfare the plunder of a captured town (women, cattle, treasure) was pooled and shared out, with special 'prizes of honour' for the leaders. The Iliad begins with a quarrel over exactly this: Agamemnon takes Briseis, Achilles' prize, and Achilles feels robbed of his time (honour). Odysseus insists that he shared 'so far as lay in me' fairly; atembomenos means 'deprived, cheated' and isē ('equal share') is a feminine noun understood with moira, 'portion'. The same line returns when the Cyclops' flocks are divided (9.549), forming a ring around the book: Odysseus presents himself as a just captain. The theme matters for Book 10, where the crew suspect him of keeping treasure for himself (10.38-45), and for his authority in Book 12.

anchor: time for the unyoking of oxen
title: 'The time for unyoking oxen': a farmer's clock
greek: ἦμος δ᾽ ἠέλιος μετενίσετο βουλυτόνδε (ēmos d' ēelios metenisseto boulytonde)
short: Homer marks late afternoon by the farmer's routine: the hour when the ploughing oxen are released.
body: Boulytos (from bous, 'ox', and lyō, 'loosen') is the time when oxen are unyoked from the plough, that is, late afternoon; the same line appears in the Iliad (Il. 16.779), where it marks the turn of the fight over the body of Cebriones. Homer has no hours, and tells time by daily activities: compare the even more striking image at 12.439-440, where the moment of Odysseus' rescue is measured by the hour when a judge rises from the assembly for his supper. Such everyday clocks bring the peaceful world of work into scenes of war and danger. Here the morning's success turns to defeat in the afternoon, a small-scale version of the day's turn in an Iliadic battle.

title: Calling the dead three times
greek: πρίν τινα τῶν δειλῶν ἑτάρων τρὶς ἕκαστον ἀῦσαι (prin tina tōn deilōn hetarōn tris hekaston aysai)
short: Before leaving, the survivors call each dead comrade three times by name, a rite for men who die and lie unburied in a foreign land.
body: The men killed by the Cicones cannot be recovered and buried. Calling each one three times seems to have been a substitute rite: it acknowledged the dead, perhaps summoned the soul to follow the ship home, and fulfilled a duty that would otherwise be left undone. The ancient explanation, preserved in the scholia, is that the soul was thus invited to come home, where a cenotaph could be built. Virgil imitates the custom when Aeneas, unable to find the body of Deiphobus, builds an empty tomb and 'thrice called aloud' to his spirit (Aeneid 6.505-506). The care for unburied comrades anticipates the request of Elpenor's ghost in Book 11 and his burial in Book 12.

title: Cape Malea: out of the known world
greek: ἀλλά με κῦμα ῥόος τε περιγνάμπτοντα Μάλειαν (alla me kyma rhoos te perignamptonta Maleian)
short: At stormy Cape Malea, the south-eastern tip of the Peloponnese, the North Wind drives Odysseus off course, out of the real Aegean into a world of wonders.
body: Malea was notorious to Greek sailors for its winds and currents (Menelaus too was driven off course there, 3.287, 4.514). Had Odysseus rounded it, he would have been a few days from Ithaca. Instead the North Wind carries him past Cythera, and after nine days on the open sea he reaches the Lotus-eaters. From this point the geography stops being mappable. Ancient readers tried hard to place every adventure (Thucydides 6.2.1 says the Cyclopes and Laestrygonians were said to be the oldest inhabitants of Sicily), but Eratosthenes famously mocked the attempt, and Merry and Riddell call the adventures a 'wonder-land' that cannot be found on a map. The 'nine days... on the tenth' pattern recurs at 10.28-29 and 12.447.

title: The Lotus-eaters (Lotophagi)
greek: Λωτοφάγοι, οἵ τ᾽ ἄνθινον εἶδαρ ἔδουσιν (Lōtophagoi, hoi t' anthinon eidar edousin)
short: A people whose 'flowery food', the lotus, makes men forget their return home; the danger is not violence but the loss of the desire for nostos.
body: The Lotus-eaters are peaceful: they 'did not plan death' for the scouts. Their threat is forgetfulness, expressed with the verb lathesthai ('forget') and the phrase nostou lathesthai, 'to forget the homeward way' (9.97, 102). Nagy reads the episode as an emblem of the whole poem: without nóos, the mind that remembers, there is no nostos. Ancient writers placed the Lotophagi on the coast of Libya (Herodotus 4.177) and identified the lotus with a sweet-fruited thorny shrub, probably the jujube (Ziziphus lotus); Merry and Riddell note Polybius' description of it and an old conjecture changing anthinon ('flowery', perhaps simply 'vegetable') to akanthinon ('thorny'). The scene invents a type that has had a long afterlife, from Tennyson's 'The Lotos-Eaters' (1832) to the English phrase 'lotus-eating'.

title: Cyclopes: the name and the race
greek: Κυκλώπων (Kyklōpōn)
short: The name was understood as 'round-eye'; Homer's shepherd Cyclopes differ from Hesiod's three divine smiths who forge Zeus' thunderbolt.
body: Hesiod's Theogony (139-146) explains the name as 'round-eyed' (kyklos, 'circle', + ōps, 'eye') and makes the Cyclopes Brontes, Steropes and Arges, sons of Earth and Sky who make Zeus' thunderbolt. Homer's Cyclopes are a whole people of giant herdsmen; strikingly, Homer never actually says that Polyphemus has only one eye, though the blinding scene implies it. Merry and Riddell survey older explanations (a solar 'eye of the universe', robbers, personified sea-forces as sons of Poseidon) and conclude that the episode belongs to a wonderland not to be found on the map; the ancients nevertheless placed the Cyclopes near Etna in Sicily (Thucydides 6.2.1). The story of a man who blinds a one-eyed giant and escapes under a ram is found in many folk traditions, a point first developed by Wilhelm Grimm (1857) and discussed by Merry and Riddell in an appendix.

title: A people without themis: the Cyclopes' way of life
greek: ὑπερφιάλων ἀθεμίστων ... τοῖσιν δ᾽ οὔτ᾽ ἀγοραὶ βουληφόροι οὔτε θέμιστες (hyperphialōn athemistōn ... toisin d' out' agorai boulēphoroi oute themistes)
short: The Cyclopes live like a Golden Age race, with crops that grow unsown, but without assemblies, laws or ships: an anti-model of the Greek city.
body: Themis is customary right, the shared rules of a community; the Cyclopes are athemistes, 'without themis', and each one 'gives law' (themisteuei) only to his own wives and children, caring nothing for his neighbours. Their land produces wheat, barley and vines without ploughing, the kind of spontaneous abundance Hesiod gives to the Golden Age, but they lack every institution the Greek audience valued: the council and assembly (agorai boulēphoroi), law, seafaring, trade and hospitality. Ancient philosophers took the passage as a picture of the earliest human society: Plato quotes it in the Laws (3.680b-c) and Aristotle in the Politics (1.1252b22) to illustrate the scattered family groups that preceded the polis. Odysseus' description prepares the test of 9.175-176: are these men just and hospitable, or savage?

anchor: a level isle that stretches aslant
title: Goat Island: a colonist's eye
greek: νῆσος ἔπειτα λάχεια (nēsos epeita lacheia)
short: Odysseus describes the uninhabited island off the Cyclopes' coast as a Greek colonist would: fertile soil, meadows for vines, a safe harbour, and fresh water.
body: The meaning of lacheia is uncertain: Murray's 'level' follows one ancient explanation; others took it as 'small' or emended the text to ou lacheia. The passage reads like a prospectus for a new settlement, and Nagy describes it as a poetic version of a ktisis, the founding of a colony, a central experience of the Greek world in the eighth and seventh centuries BC. The island is wasted because the Cyclopes have no ships and no shipwrights 'who would have made of this isle also a fair settlement'. The contrast between nature and culture runs through the Cyclops episode: the Cyclopes enjoy nature's gifts without the arts (technē) that make a civilised life. The detail that 'some god guided us' through a moonless night (9.142-145) adds a sense of divine purpose.

sources.cite: Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Odyssey Rhapsody 9', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2017, rev. 2018, comment on O.09.106-141 and O.09.133

title: 'Ships with vermilion cheeks'
greek: νέες ... μιλτοπάρῃοι (nees ... miltoparēioi)
short: A fixed epithet for ships: their bows, the 'cheeks', were painted with red pigment (miltos), probably red ochre or cinnabar.
body: Homer often describes ships by the colour of their bows: 'red-cheeked' here and in the Iliad (Il. 2.637, of Odysseus' own ships), 'purple-cheeked' (phoinikoparēioi, 11.124), 'dark-prowed' (kyanoprōiroi, 9.482). Merry and Riddell cite Herodotus 3.58 for the old custom of painting ships red, and observe that the epithet is purely conventional here, since the point of the sentence is that the Cyclopes have no ships at all. This is a good example of the 'generic' epithet in oral poetry, used for the type of thing rather than for the particular case. Nagy suggests that the alternation of red and purple may even reflect different traditions of performance.

title: The test of xenia: savage or god-fearing?
greek: ἤ ῥ᾽ οἵ γ᾽ ὑβρισταί τε καὶ ἄγριοι οὐδὲ δίκαιοι, / ἦε φιλόξεινοι, καί σφιν νόος ἐστὶ θεουδής (ē rh' hoi g' hybristai te kai agrioi oude dikaioi, ēe philoxeinoi, kai sphin noos esti theoudēs)
short: Odysseus' question, also asked on Scheria and on Ithaca, sums up the Odyssey's moral test of any society: do its people respect strangers and the gods?
body: The same pair of lines appears when Odysseus wakes on Scheria (6.120-121) and again on Ithaca (13.201-202), so the question is a structuring formula of the poem. Xenia, 'guest-friendship', was a sacred institution: a stranger was to be received, washed, fed and only then asked his name, and sent on with gifts (xeinia). Each society Odysseus meets can be measured against this ideal: the Phaeacians fulfil it lavishly, the suitors in Ithaca abuse it, and the Cyclops turns it into a grotesque parody, eating his guests and promising Odysseus the 'gift' of being eaten last (9.369-370). Murray's 'cruel, and wild, and unjust' renders hybristai, agrioi and ou dikaioi; hybris, violent arrogance, is the vice of the suitors too.

title: Maro, priest of Apollo, and his wine
greek: Μάρων, Εὐάνθεος υἱός, ἱρεὺς Ἀπόλλωνος (Marōn, Euantheos huios, hireus Apollōnos)
short: A priest whom Odysseus spared at Ismarus gave him a wine so strong that it was mixed with twenty measures of water; it becomes the weapon against the Cyclops.
body: Odysseus' respect for Apollo's priest at Ismarus (contrast Agamemnon's treatment of Chryses in Iliad 1) earns him gold, a silver mixing-bowl and twelve jars of unmixed wine. Greeks normally drank wine diluted with water, often three parts water to one of wine (Hesiod, Works and Days 596); a wine that could take twenty measures is a marvel. Maro later gave his name to Maroneia in Thrace, famous for wine, and later poets made him a son of Dionysus (Euripides, Cyclops 141), while Merry and Riddell note that another tradition made Euanthes ('fair-flowering') Dionysus' son. The detail that only Maro, his wife and one housekeeper knew of the wine adds to its mystique. Polyphemus, who knows only rustic wine, drinks it unmixed and calls it 'a streamlet of ambrosia and nectar' (9.359).

title: Odysseus' curiosity and the hope of guest-gifts
greek: ὄφρ᾽ αὐτόν τε ἴδοιμι, καὶ εἴ μοι ξείνια δοίη (ophr' auton te idoimi, kai ei moi xeinia doiē)
short: Against his men's advice Odysseus waits in the cave to see its owner and receive guest-gifts, a decision he admits 'would have been better far' not to make.
body: Xeinia were the gifts a host gave a departing guest, the material sign of a lasting bond of guest-friendship; Odysseus has just received many from the Phaeacians (8.389-420). His wish to meet the Cyclops combines a hero's curiosity, the desire for profit, and confidence in the rules of hospitality. The narrator Odysseus judges his younger self severely: 'it would have been better far' (9.228). Readers have debated how far Odysseus is responsible for the deaths of his men here; Eurylochus later blames the losses on Odysseus' 'folly' (atasthaliai, 10.437), the same word the proem uses for the crew's own crime (1.7). The Cyclops will twist the custom: his only 'guest-gift' is to eat Odysseus last (9.370).

title: 'Are you pirates?'
greek: ἦ τι κατὰ πρῆξιν ἦ μαψιδίως ἀλάλησθε / οἷά τε ληιστῆρες (ē ti kata prēxin ē mapsidiōs alalēsthe hoia te lēistēres)
short: The Cyclops greets his visitors with the standard question asked of seafarers, the same lines Nestor uses to Telemachus at 3.71-74.
body: Prēxis here means trading business; the alternative is roving 'at random' as pirates (lēistēres) who 'bring evil to men of other lands'. Thucydides, describing early Greek history, notes that piracy was then no disgrace, and that the old poets show people asking arriving sailors whether they are pirates without any insult being meant (Thucydides 1.5.2). The irony here is double. The question comes, word for word, from a polite host in Book 3, but now it is spoken by a cannibal; and Odysseus has in fact just sacked Ismarus, a raid that a Thracian would certainly call piracy. Odysseus answers by presenting his men as Agamemnon's soldiers and as suppliants.

title: Zeus Xeinios, protector of strangers and suppliants
greek: Ζεὺς δ᾽ ἐπιτιμήτωρ ἱκετάων τε ξείνων τε, / ξείνιος (Zeus d' epitimētōr hiketaōn te xeinōn te, xeinios)
short: Odysseus appeals to Zeus as avenger of suppliants and strangers; the Cyclops replies that his people care nothing for Zeus.
body: Xeinios ('of strangers') is one of Zeus' cult titles: the god protects guests and their hosts, and Hiketēsios protects suppliants (hiketai), those who come clasping knees and asking for protection. Odysseus combines both claims: his men are strangers and suppliants, and Zeus is their epitimētōr, 'avenger, one who exacts the penalty'. Polyphemus' answer (9.273-278) is the clearest statement of impiety in Homer: the Cyclopes 'reck not of Zeus... since verily we are better far than they'. After the blinding Odysseus taunts him that 'Zeus has taken vengeance on thee, and the other gods' (9.479). Yet Zeus does not accept Odysseus' sacrifice at the end of the book (9.553-555), so the episode raises the question of whose side the gods are on.

anchor: a black ship of twenty oars
title: The club like a ship's mast
greek: ὅσσον θ᾽ ἱστὸν νηὸς ἐεικοσόροιο μελαίνης, / φορτίδος εὐρείης (hosson th' histon nēos eeikosoroio melainēs, phortidos eureiēs)
short: The Cyclops' olive club is compared to the mast of a broad merchant ship, one of several images from seafaring and craft in the episode.
body: A phortis was a beamy cargo vessel, as opposed to a warship; the comparison gives the giant's scale through the familiar world of the Greek sailor. Odysseus turns the club into a stake: he cuts off a fathom, has it smoothed, sharpens and fire-hardens it, and hides it in the dung. The sequence is a small display of technē, practical craft, the very thing the Cyclopes lack (no shipwrights, 9.126). The similes of the blinding continue the theme: the stake is worked like a shipwright's drill, and the eye hisses like iron quenched by a smith (9.384-394). The narrative thus sets human skill against monstrous strength (biē).

title: Outis, 'Noman'
greek: Οὖτις ἐμοί γ᾽ ὄνομα· Οὖτιν δέ με κικλήσκουσι (Outis emoi g' onoma; Outin de me kiklēskousi)
short: Odysseus gives his name as Outis, 'Nobody': a trick that works because the Cyclops treats it as a proper name.
body: Outis is the ordinary Greek for 'no one'. Merry and Riddell note that the accusative Outin is formed differently from the ordinary accusative of the pronoun (outina), as befits a proper name. The trick pays off at 9.408 and 9.410: when Polyphemus cries 'Noman is slaying me', his neighbours hear 'no one is killing me' and go home. Nagy observes the cost: by becoming 'Nobody' the hero gives up the kleos attached to his real name, which is why he cannot resist reclaiming it as he sails away (9.502-505).

title: The Cyclops' 'guest-gift'
greek: τὸ δέ τοι ξεινήιον ἔσται (to de toi xeinēion estai)
short: Polyphemus promises Noman a guest-gift and then reveals it: he will be eaten last. Hospitality is turned inside out.
body: Xeinēion is the formal gift a host gives a guest; Polyphemus asks Odysseus' name so as to give him one (9.355-356), exactly as a proper host would. The 'gift' is a monstrous joke, and the scene is the sharpest perversion of xenia in the poem: the host eats his guests instead of feeding them. There is a corresponding perversion in Ithaca, where Ctesippus throws an ox-hoof at the disguised Odysseus and calls it a xeinion (20.296-300). Odysseus' taunt after the escape makes the point explicit: the Cyclops 'didst not shrink from eating thy guests in thine own house' (9.477-479).

title: The shipwright's drill
greek: ὡς ὅτε τις τρυπῷ δόρυ νήιον ἀνὴρ / τρυπάνῳ (hōs hote tis trypōi dory nēion anēr trypanōi)
short: Odysseus twists the stake in the eye as a shipwright works a bow-drill, his men below spinning it with a thong.
body: The trypanon was a bow- or strap-drill: one man pressed down from above while others pulled a thong wound round the shaft back and forth, so that it spun 'unceasingly'. The simile maps exactly onto the scene: Odysseus leans on the stake from above, his four companions turn it. The image comes from shipbuilding, the craft the Cyclopes lack, and Odysseus himself is a skilled craftsman who bores timbers when he builds his raft (5.246-248) and his marriage-bed (23.196-201). The gruesome detail that follows (blood, singed brows, crackling roots of the eye) is unusually physical for Homer.

anchor: a smith dips a great axe
title: The smith quenching iron
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἀνὴρ χαλκεὺς πέλεκυν μέγαν ἠὲ σκέπαρνον / εἰν ὕδατι ψυχρῷ βάπτῃ ... τὸ γὰρ αὖτε σιδήρου γε κράτος ἐστίν (hōs d' hot' anēr chalkeus pelekyn megan ēe skeparnon ein hydati psychrōi baptēi ... to gar aute sidērou ge kratos estin)
short: The eye hisses round the burning stake like a red-hot axe-head plunged into cold water by a smith to temper it.
body: This is one of the clearest references in Homer to the working of iron: quenching hot iron in water hardens it, and the narrator explains that 'therefrom comes the strength of iron'. Heroes in the poems fight with bronze, but the similes, drawn from the poet's own world, show iron tools in daily use, one of the signs that the epics took shape in the early Iron Age. The smith is still called chalkeus, 'bronze-worker', an old word that survived the change of metal. Nagy connects the simile with myths of the invention of technology, which suits an episode in which craft defeats brute force. Together with the drill simile it makes the blinding an act of human technē.

title: Polyphemus, son of Poseidon
greek: Πολύφημος (Polyphēmos)
short: The Cyclops is named only when his neighbours call to him; the name means 'much-spoken-of' or 'of many voices', ironic for a monster outwitted by words.
body: Polyphēmos combines poly- ('much') and phēmē ('speech, report, fame'), so it can mean 'famous' or 'loud-voiced'; the same name belongs to a Lapith hero in the Iliad (Il. 1.264). Nagy takes the name to mean 'having many different things said' and ties it to the coded speech (ainos) at which Odysseus excels; the Cyclops, whose name promises words, is beaten by a pun. The proem of the poem already told us that Poseidon is angry because Odysseus blinded his son Polyphemus, born of the nymph Thoosa (1.68-73). The episode has many folk-tale parallels, but Homer gives his giant some individual traits, above all the tender speech to his ram (9.447-460). Later poets made him a lovesick figure wooing Galatea (Theocritus, Idyll 11; Ovid, Metamorphoses 13).

title: Mē tis and mētis: the great pun
greek: εἰ μὲν δὴ μή τίς σε βιάζεται ... ὡς ὄνομ᾽ ἐξαπάτησεν ἐμὸν καὶ μῆτις ἀμύμων (ei men dē mē tis se biazetai ... hōs onom' exapatēsen emon kai mētis amymōn)
short: The neighbours answer 'if no one (mē tis) is harming you'; Odysseus laughs that his name and his mētis, 'cunning intelligence', have deceived them.
body: In Greek, 'no one' can be outis or, in conditional and other clauses, mē tis. When the Cyclopes reply 'if no one (mē tis) is doing violence to you' (9.410), the phrase sounds exactly like mētis, the word for cunning intelligence that defines Odysseus (he is polymētis, 'of many counsels'). Odysseus then states it outright: 'my name and my faultless mētis deceived' (9.414). English cannot keep the pun; Murray's 'cunning device' renders mētis. Polyphemus himself complains that Noman beat him 'by guile (dolōi) and not by force (biē)' (9.408), naming the central opposition of the episode, mētis versus biē. Nagy argues that the trick wins Odysseus' nostos while costing him his name, and so his kleos.

title: Polyphemus speaks to his ram
greek: κριὲ πέπον (krie pepon)
short: The blinded giant addresses his favourite ram, which carries Odysseus beneath it, in a speech of unexpected pathos.
body: Pepon (Murray's 'Good') is a word of affection, literally 'ripe, soft', used in the Iliad between dear companions. The giant notices that the ram, always the first to the pasture, the river and the fold, is the last to leave, and imagines that it grieves for its master's eye. The dramatic irony is intense: Odysseus is clinging to the fleece and hears every word, including the threat to dash his brains out. The scene makes the monster sympathetic for a moment, and shows that his solitary life has an emotional centre in his flock. The ram is then given to Odysseus as his special share and sacrificed to Zeus (9.550-553). The escape under the ram's belly is one of the most widespread folk-tale motifs attached to the blinded giant.

title: Odysseus reveals his name
greek: φάσθαι Ὀδυσσῆα πτολιπόρθιον ἐξαλαῶσαι, / υἱὸν Λαέρτεω, Ἰθάκῃ ἔνι οἰκί᾽ ἔχοντα (phasthai Odyssēa ptoliporthion exalaōsai, huion Laerteō, Ithakēi eni oiki' echonta)
short: Ignoring his men's pleas, Odysseus shouts his full name, title, father and home to the Cyclops, giving him what he needs for a curse.
body: Odysseus reclaims the name he had suppressed as 'Noman', with all the elements of heroic identity: personal name, epithet ptoliporthios ('sacker of cities'), patronymic and homeland. The impulse is the Iliadic hero's need for kleos: a victory is worthless if no one knows who won it. But it is a disastrous mistake, the counterpart to the trick that saved him: a curse in the ancient world needed the victim's name, and Polyphemus uses every detail Odysseus supplied in his prayer to Poseidon (9.530-531). The giant also reveals a prophecy by the seer Telemus that he would be blinded by Odysseus (9.507-512), a typical motif of the oracle fulfilled when it is too late. Nagy sees in the scene the tension between mētis, which brings survival, and kleos, which demands a name.

title: Polyphemus' curse
greek: κλῦθι, Ποσείδαον γαιήοχε κυανοχαῖτα (klythi, Poseidaon gaiēoche kyanochaita)
short: The Cyclops' prayer sets out the rest of the plot: Odysseus will come home late, alone, on another's ship, to find trouble in his house.
body: The prayer has the regular form of a Greek prayer: an invocation with titles ('earth-holder', gaiēochos, and 'dark-haired', kyanochaitēs), a claim on the god (here sonship rather than past sacrifices), and a request. Polyphemus first asks that Odysseus never reach home, then adds a fall-back request that, if he is fated to return, he come, in Murray's words, 'late may he come and in evil case, after losing all his comrades, in a ship that is another's; and may he find woes in his house'. Every element comes true: the crew perishes in Book 12, the Phaeacians carry him home on their ship in Book 13, and the suitors fill his halls. Teiresias repeats the same terms almost word for word (11.114-115), and Circe confirms them (12.141). The curse is the origin of Poseidon's anger announced in the proem (1.20-21, 1.68-75).

title: Zeus rejects the sacrifice
greek: ὁ δ᾽ οὐκ ἐμπάζετο ἱρῶν, / ἀλλ᾽ ἄρα μερμήριζεν ὅπως ἀπολοίατο πᾶσαι / νῆες (ho d' ouk empazeto hirōn, all' ara mermērizen hopōs apoloiato pasai nēes)
short: Odysseus burns the thigh-pieces of the ram to Zeus, but the god 'heeded not': he was already planning the destruction of all the ships.
body: The ram, given to Odysseus as a special share 'apart' (exaireton) in the fair division of the flocks, is sacrificed to Zeus Kronides 'who is lord of all'. Burning the thigh-bones wrapped in fat was the gods' portion in a Greek animal sacrifice. The statement that Zeus refused it is striking because Odysseus has just claimed that Zeus punished the Cyclops. Scholars disagree about what it means: some see Zeus respecting his brother Poseidon's claim, others think it is the narrating Odysseus' hindsight on the disasters that followed, and others see a hint that the gods' plans are simply beyond human calculation. Only Odysseus survives, as the proem says. The book ends with the formula of grieving survivors (9.565-566), framing the episode as the Cicones episode was framed.
